summary:
AgroShift is a data-driven agricultural decision-support tool developed to help farmers plan crop rotations under climate variability and water constraints.

Our main contribution is a data science pipeline that integrates 21 years of NASA POWER climate observations, USDA soil surveys, and FAO crop requirements. We applied data preprocessing, quality filtering, feature engineering, and machine learning to forecast monthly rainfall, comparing Ridge Regression, Gradient Boosting, and a seasonal baseline through chronological validation.

We then developed a multicriteria optimization model that evaluates crop suitability, irrigation demand, historical rainfall scenarios, and crop rotation sequences. Using a bounded search algorithm, the system ranks alternatives according to environmental constraints and farmer-defined priorities.

AgroShift transforms complex environmental datasets into transparent, explainable agricultural recommendations, demonstrating how predictive modeling and mathematical optimization can support more informed and climate-resilient farming decisions.
details:
What does AgroShift do?

AgroShift is a web-based agricultural decision-support system that combines Earth observation data, machine learning, and mathematical optimization to help farmers explore crop rotation strategies under changing environmental conditions.

Rather than recommending crops based on a single variable, our system evaluates how climate, soil properties, water availability, planting schedules, and agricultural priorities interact. Its main contribution is a data science pipeline that transforms environmental information into explainable, personalized crop rotation alternatives.

Data Sources and Processing

We integrated three major scientific data sources:

  • NASA POWER: Historical observations of precipitation, temperature, solar radiation, humidity-related variables, wind speed, and atmospheric pressure. We used 21 complete years of historical climate data to develop and evaluate rainfall forecasting models.
  • USDA SSURGO and Web Soil Survey: Soil properties, including pH, salinity, texture, and available water capacity. Our geospatial analysis evaluates soil information across the field polygon rather than relying exclusively on its center point.
  • FAO ECOCROP and FAO-56: Environmental requirements, growing periods, crop coefficients, rooting characteristics, and reference evapotranspiration methods.

Data quality was an important part of our methodology. Starting with 2,568 ECOCROP records, we applied completeness and consistency requirements to establish a catalog of 37 eligible crops with documented characteristics for the recommendation process.

Machine Learning and Predictive Modeling

One of our main technical contributions is the development and evaluation of a monthly rainfall forecasting pipeline.

We implemented and compared three predictive approaches: a seasonal average baseline, Ridge Regression with L2 regularization, and Gradient Boosting Regression.

Our features include seasonal patterns, temporal trends, and lagged precipitation values. We used chronological validation rather than random data splitting to reduce data leakage and evaluate predictions using historical information available at each forecasting point.

In our documented evaluation, Ridge Regression achieved the lowest validation Mean Absolute Error (MAE), approximately 7.27 mm/month, compared with 7.44 mm/month for Gradient Boosting and 8.07 mm/month for the seasonal baseline.

This comparison illustrates an important aspect of our approach: model selection is based on measured validation performance, not algorithmic complexity. These results evaluate rainfall predictions, not crop yield or future harvest success.

Mathematical Modeling and Optimization

Rainfall prediction is only one component of AgroShift. Our main objective is to convert climatic information into useful agricultural decisions.

We implemented a multicriteria decision model that evaluates five dimensions: water, climate, soil, crop diversity, and rotation quality.

To estimate crop water requirements, we use the FAO-56 reference evapotranspiration methodology and crop coefficients. The system also evaluates irrigation demand under historical rainfall scenarios and compares it with the farmer's available water budget.

We developed a bounded beam-search algorithm to explore sequences of complete crop cycles, considering growing periods, preparation intervals, crop compatibility, and water constraints. Rather than evaluating only individual crops, AgroShift analyzes entire planting strategies.

Each alternative receives a weighted score based on the farmer's selected priorities. The system can return up to six ranked alternatives, including crop rotations and monoculture strategies, accompanied by water-demand estimates and relevant warnings.

The optimization is approximate, and its scores represent comparative decision criteria rather than probabilities of agricultural success.

Technology and Implementation

We developed AgroShift using Python, FastAPI, NumPy, scikit-learn, React, JavaScript, and Vite.

Python handles climate data processing, statistical modeling, geospatial analysis, agronomic calculations, and optimization. FastAPI connects the analytical backend to the web application through REST endpoints. React provides the interactive interface, allowing farmers to outline their fields on a map, specify water availability, select agricultural priorities, and review the resulting alternatives.

We also incorporated geospatial soil datasets, GeoJSON-based field geometry, and scientific reference databases to connect geographic information with the recommendation engine.

Creativity and Intended Impact

What makes AgroShift different is the integration of predictive modeling with explainable agricultural optimization.

A rainfall forecast alone cannot determine what a farmer should plant. Likewise, selecting a crop that matches local temperature conditions does not guarantee that it fits the available water budget or contributes to a suitable rotation.

Our approach connects these separate problems into a single decision process. By combining NASA observations, soil characteristics, crop requirements, historical climate scenarios, and farmer-defined priorities, AgroShift allows users to explore trade-offs rather than receive one unexplained recommendation.

The intended impact is to make scientific environmental information more accessible for agricultural planning, especially where water limitations and climate variability complicate decisions.

AgroShift remains a prototype. Its recommendations have not yet been validated through field trials, and its predictive results do not guarantee future yields or water savings. Nevertheless, the project demonstrates how data engineering, machine learning, geospatial analysis, and constrained optimization can work together to support more transparent, informed, and potentially climate-resilient agricultural decisions.
